meta.howTextWasRead: Each performance expectation page was read through a web fetch tool that summarizes pages, and the statement was copied back in short pieces. Twice-read items (the page and a topic overview page, or the page twice, with identical wording): 2-LS4-1, 3-LS3-1, 3-LS3-2, 3-LS4-1 to 3-LS4-4, MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2, MS-LS4-1 to MS-LS4-6, HS-LS2-8, HS-LS3-1 to HS-LS3-3 and HS-LS4-1 to HS-LS4-6. Read once: 1-LS3-1, 3-LS2-1, MS-ESS1-4, MS-LS1-4, MS-LS1-5, MS-LS2-1 and HS-ESS2-7. A direct download of the pages was refused by the site (HTTP 403), so no file copy exists. The foundation box names (practice, core idea, crosscutting concept) come from the same reads. Nobody has compared the wording with the printed standards.

levels.2: Covers the idea without the word

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Patterns
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: Noticing patterns in nature and using them to sort things, describe events and look for causes.

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Cause and Effect
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: Looking for what causes an event, how the cause leads to the effect, and whether a link is a cause or a coincidence.

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: What a thing looks like and how it behaves can depend on its size, its time span and the amount of it.
crosscuttingConcepts.germanMatch: none found (the German list has system levels in its goal tags, which is a loose relative)

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Systems and System Models
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: Treating a set of parts that work together as a system, and using models to describe how its parts interact.
crosscuttingConcepts.germanMatch: none found (loosely related to the German system levels)

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Energy and Matter
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: Following energy and matter as they flow through a system and cycle within it.

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Structure and Function
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: How the shape and makeup of something relates to what it does.

crosscuttingConcepts.name: Stability and Change
crosscuttingConcepts.definition: What stays steady and what changes in a system, and why.
crosscuttingConcepts.germanMatch: Steuerung und Regelung, Individuelle Entwicklung and Evolutive Entwicklung (partly)

evolutionConcepts.def: Individuals in a population differ in their traits: in their genes, in how they look and in how they behave. This variation is the starting point for any form of selection and so for evolution.
Differences in the DNA sequence between individuals of a population. They arise through mutation, recombination and gene transfer.
Visible differences in traits between individuals. They come from genetic variation, from the environment, or from both together.
A change of the phenotype that is caused by the environment and is not inherited. It stays within the range that the genome allows.
New combinations of the parents' alleles during sexual reproduction (meiosis, crossing-over). It is a main source of genetic variation without new mutations.
Transfer of genetic material between organisms outside normal inheritance from parent to offspring (horizontal gene transfer). It matters most in bacteria.
Heritable changes in gene activity (for example through DNA methylation) that leave the DNA sequence itself unchanged.
The ability of one genotype to produce different phenotypes under different environmental conditions.
Traits pass from one generation to the next through several channels, some of them outside the genes.
Traits pass from parents to offspring through the DNA sequence.
Patterns of gene activity pass on over generations while the DNA sequence stays the same.
Behaviors, knowledge and skills pass on through watching, copying and teaching instead of through genes.
Offspring inherit an environment that their parents changed. This is a channel of inheritance next to the genes and is closely tied to niche construction.
Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more often in a given environment. This difference in reproductive success drives change in populations over generations.
Selection that disfavors extreme trait values and favors the middle of the range.
Selection that favors one extreme of a trait and shifts the population average in one direction over generations.
Selection that keeps genetic variation in a population, for example because individuals with two different alleles have an advantage.
How much a trait helps depends on how common it already is in the population.
Evolutionary compromises. A trait helps in one way and costs in another, so no trait can be best at everything at once.
Selection through differences in mating success that come from mate choice or from competition for mates, whatever the effect on survival.
A measure of how much a genotype or phenotype contributes to the gene pool of the next generation through survival and reproduction. It differs from everyday physical fitness.

Traits that arose by natural selection because they raised survival or reproductive success in a particular environment. The pair of words covers the process (adaptation) and the result (adaptedness).
The job a trait does for its bearer, which selection can explain.

evolutionConcepts.en: Exaptation (traits taking on a new function)
evolutionConcepts.def: A trait that arose for another function (or for none) and later took on a new function.
An adaptation no longer fits the current environment because the environment changed faster than the adaptation could, for example through cultural change.
Random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, independent of any advantage. It acts most strongly in small populations.
Exchange of genetic material between populations when individuals move in or out. It works against differences between populations.
A sudden, strong drop in the genetic diversity of a population after an event that leaves only a small, unrepresentative part of it alive.
Lower genetic diversity in a newly founded population that descends from a small number of founders of a larger source population.
Theory about how evolution shapes the timing of growth, reproduction and aging under limited resources, including the trade-off between the number of offspring and the investment in each.
Species adapt to each other over time. Changes in one species create selection pressure on the other.
A special case of coevolution in which people steer the evolution of crops and domestic animals through deliberate or unintended artificial selection.
Organisms change their environment and with it the conditions of selection for themselves and for other species.
Selection can act at several levels of biological organization at the same time, from genes and cells to individuals and groups.
Theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that were taken up by ancestors of cells with a nucleus and became organelles.

evolutionConcepts.en: Evolution from single cells to multicellular life
evolutionConcepts.def: The transition from single-celled to multicellular organisms with specialized, cooperating cells. It happened several times independently.
Selection that favors helping genetic relatives, because helping them passes on copies of one's own genes (relatedness times benefit greater than cost).
Explanation of how cooperative and seemingly selfless behavior can arise and stay stable through selection despite its cost to the individual.
Selection-like processes between cells or cell lines inside one organism.
The idea of the huge spans of Earth and life history, far beyond everyday experience, which make evolutionary change possible.
The division of Earth history into time spans (for example Cambrian, Cretaceous, Cenozoic) that give a frame for placing evolutionary events.
Preserved remains or traces of past organisms. They are direct material evidence for the history of life and how it changed over time.
Fossils that combine traits of an ancestral group and a descendant group and so show gradual evolutionary transitions.
Diagrams and methods that show relationships between groups of organisms based on shared derived traits.
The basic principle that all living species descend from common ancestors and so are linked in a single branching tree of life.

evolutionConcepts.de: Konservierung von Merkmalen (gemeinsame genetische Grundlagen, Baupläne, Entwicklungsprozesse usw.)
evolutionConcepts.en: Conservation of traits (shared genetic basis, body plans, developmental processes and so on)
evolutionConcepts.def: Basic genetic control mechanisms, body plans and developmental processes stay surprisingly similar over very long periods and across distant animal groups.

evolutionConcepts.de: Homologie und Analogie/Konvergente und divergente Evolution
evolutionConcepts.en: Homology and analogy / convergent and divergent evolution
evolutionConcepts.def: Homologous structures go back to a shared pattern in an ancestor (divergent evolution). Analogous structures arose independently with a similar function (convergent evolution).
The process by which one or more new species arise from an ancestral species, often through geographic isolation. Adaptive radiation is the quick split into many ecologically specialized species.
The final disappearance of a species when no individual survives. It is a constant part of evolutionary history and speeds up during mass extinctions.
A research field that asks how changes in the genetic programs of individual development lead to evolutionary changes in body plans.

Haeckel's historical claim that the development of an individual repeats the evolutionary history of its group. In this strict form it has been refuted. Modern evo-devo replaces it with the idea of shared but modified developmental programs.

Change in knowledge, behavior, tools and social practices over generations through learning, transmission and selection among cultural variants. It resembles biological evolution but has mechanisms of its own.

items.shortLabel: Offspring look like their parents but differ
items.text: Make observations to construct an evidence-based account that young plants and animals are like, but not exactly like, their parents.
items.why: Young organisms look like their parents but differ in small ways. That is inheritance and variation, two things evolution needs. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Compare the diversity of life in habitats
items.text: Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
items.why: Students compare how many kinds of life live in different habitats. This is background for later work on diversity and adaptation. The text says nothing about change over generations.

items.shortLabel: Group living helps animals survive
items.text: Construct an argument that some animals form groups that help members survive.
coreIdeas: LS2.D: Social Interactions and Group Behavior
items.why: Group living helps members survive. The benefits of living in groups are one starting point for the evolution of cooperation. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Traits are inherited and vary within a group
items.text: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence that plants and animals have traits inherited from parents and that variation of these traits exists in a group of similar organisms.
items.why: Students find that traits are inherited and that individuals in a group vary. Inheritance and variation are two of the conditions for natural selection. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: The environment can shape traits
items.text: Use evidence to support the explanation that traits can be influenced by the environment.
items.why: Students see that the environment can shape a trait. This helps separate inherited variation from changes caused by the environment, a common point of confusion in evolution teaching. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Fossils show organisms and places of long ago
items.text: Analyze and interpret data from fossils to provide evidence of the organisms and the environments in which they lived long ago.
coreIdeas: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
items.why: Fossils are evidence of organisms and places of long ago. This is the first step toward the fossil record and deep time. The text does not use the word evolution.

items.shortLabel: Variation can help survival and reproduction
items.text: Use evidence to construct an explanation for how the variations in characteristics among individuals of the same species may provide advantages in surviving, finding mates, and reproducing.
items.why: Variation among individuals can help them survive, find mates and reproduce. This is the core of natural selection in everyday words. The words natural selection and evolution do not appear.

items.shortLabel: Some organisms survive a habitat better
items.text: Construct an argument with evidence that in a particular habitat some organisms can survive well, some survive less well, and some cannot survive at all.
items.why: Some organisms survive a habitat well and others less well. This is differences in survival, the second step of natural selection. The text does not name natural selection or evolution.

items.shortLabel: Solutions when a habitat changes
items.text: Make a claim about the merit of a solution to a problem caused when the environment changes and the types of plants and animals that live there may change.
coreIdeas: LS2.C: Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience
items.why: Students judge a solution to a problem caused by a changing habitat. It is background for ideas about selection pressure but does not teach them. The standard marks it with an asterisk because it also connects to engineering.

items.shortLabel: The geologic time scale and rock layers
items.text: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence from rock strata for how the geologic time scale is used to organize Earth's 4.6-billion-year-old history.
coreIdeas: ESS1.C: The History of Planet Earth
items.why: Students use rock layers to explain the geologic time scale. Evolution happens on that time scale. The text does not mention life or evolution.

items.shortLabel: Behaviors and plant structures affect reproduction
items.text: Use argument based on empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support an explanation for how characteristic animal behaviors and specialized plant structures affect the probability of successful reproduction of animals and plants respectively.
coreIdeas: LS1.B: Growth and Development of Organisms
items.why: Animal behaviors and plant structures change the chance of successful reproduction. This is the idea behind fitness. The text does not mention selection or evolution.

items.shortLabel: Environment and genes shape growth
items.text: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for how environmental and genetic factors influence the growth of organisms.
coreIdeas: LS1.B: Growth and Development of Organisms
items.why: Environmental and genetic factors both shape growth. This is background for telling inherited differences from differences caused by the environment.

items.shortLabel: Resource availability affects populations
items.text: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence for the effects of resource availability on organisms and populations of organisms in an ecosystem.
items.why: Limited resources affect organisms and populations. Competition for resources is one cause of selection pressure. The text is about ecosystems at one point in time and does not mention change over generations.

items.shortLabel: Gene mutations affect proteins and traits
items.text: Develop and use a model to describe why structural changes to genes (mutations) located on chromosomes may affect proteins and may result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects to the structure and function of the organism.
items.why: Mutations change proteins and can have harmful, helpful or neutral effects. Mutations are a source of new variation. The text does not link them to evolution.

items.shortLabel: Sexual and asexual reproduction and variation
items.text: Develop and use a model to describe why asexual reproduction results in offspring with identical genetic information and sexual reproduction results in offspring with genetic variation.
coreIdeas: LS1.B: Growth and Development of Organisms
items.why: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with genetic variation and asexual reproduction does not. This explains one source of the variation that selection works on. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: The fossil record shows change of life forms
items.text: Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of life forms throughout the history of life on Earth under the assumption that natural laws operate today as in the past.
coreIdeas: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
items.why: The fossil record shows that life forms appeared, changed and went extinct across Earth's history. This is evidence for evolution. The text does not use the word evolution.

items.shortLabel: Anatomy shows evolutionary relationships
items.text: Apply scientific ideas to construct an explanation for the anatomical similarities and differences among modern organisms and between modern and fossil organisms to infer evolutionary relationships.
coreIdeas: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
items.why: Anatomical similarities between organisms, including fossils, are used to infer evolutionary relationships. The text names evolutionary relationships directly.

items.shortLabel: Embryo similarities show relationships
items.text: Analyze displays of pictorial data to compare patterns of similarities in the embryological development across multiple species to identify relationships not evident in the fully formed anatomy.
coreIdeas: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
items.why: Similarities in embryo development across species point to shared ancestry. The text does not use the word evolution.

items.shortLabel: Genetic variation raises survival chances
items.text: Construct an explanation based on evidence that describes how genetic variations of traits in a population increase some individuals’ probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment.
items.why: Genetic variation raises some individuals' chances of surviving and reproducing in a given environment. This describes natural selection without naming it.

items.shortLabel: Technologies that change which traits are inherited
items.text: Gather and synthesize information about technologies that have changed the way humans influence the inheritance of desired traits in organisms.
items.why: Technologies such as selective breeding change how humans influence which traits are passed on. This is artificial selection. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Mathematical models of natural selection
items.text: Use mathematical representations to support explanations of how natural selection may lead to increases and decreases of specific traits in populations over time.
items.why: Students use mathematics to explain how natural selection changes how common traits are in populations. The text names natural selection.

items.shortLabel: Earth's systems and life coevolve
items.text: Construct an argument based on evidence about the simultaneous coevolution of Earth’s systems and life on Earth.
items.why: The text names the coevolution of Earth's systems and life. The German concept of coevolution is about species adapting to each other, so the match is loose.

items.shortLabel: Group behavior and the chance to survive
items.text: Evaluate evidence for the role of group behavior on individual and species’ chances to survive and reproduce.
coreIdeas: LS2.D: Social Interactions and Group Behavior
items.why: Students judge whether group behavior changes the chances to survive and reproduce for individuals and for species. This is the multilevel selection question. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: DNA and chromosomes code inherited traits
items.text: Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring.
items.why: Students ask how DNA and chromosomes code the traits that parents pass on. Inheritance is a condition for evolution. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Sources of inheritable genetic variation
items.text: Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, and/or (3) mutations caused by environmental factors.
items.why: Students defend claims about three sources of inheritable variation: meiosis, copying errors and mutations. Variation is the raw material of evolution. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Variation and distribution of traits in populations
items.text: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.
items.why: Students explain how variation in traits is spread across a population. Variation within populations is what selection acts on. The text does not mention evolution.

items.shortLabel: Evidence for common ancestry and evolution
items.text: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.
coreIdeas: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
items.why: The text names biological evolution and common ancestry and asks for the evidence behind them.

items.shortLabel: Four factors behind evolution
items.text: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.
items.why: The text names the process of evolution and lists four factors for it.

items.shortLabel: Advantageous heritable traits become more common
items.text: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait.
items.why: Organisms with an advantageous heritable trait increase in proportion. This is natural selection described with statistics. The words natural selection and evolution do not appear.

items.shortLabel: Natural selection leads to adaptation
items.text: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.
items.why: The text names natural selection and asks how it leads to adaptation of populations.

items.shortLabel: Environmental change, new species and extinction
items.text: Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in (1) increases in the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of other species.
items.why: Students weigh evidence that changes in the environment can increase some species, produce new species and cause extinctions. Speciation and extinction are central evolution ideas. The text does not use the word evolution.

items.shortLabel: Reduce human harm to biodiversity
items.text: Create or revise a simulation to test a solution to mitigate adverse impacts of human activity on biodiversity.
items.why: This is a design task about reducing human harm to biodiversity. Extinction is the only evolution idea it touches. The standard marks it with an asterisk because it connects to engineering.

threads.title: Variation, inheritance and selection from grade 1 to grade 12
threads.connectingIdea: How does the idea that offspring differ a little from their parents grow into an explanation of natural selection?
threads.narrative: The path starts in grade 1 with young plants and animals that look like their parents but differ in small ways. In grade 3 students link variation to survival and reproduction. In middle school they add genes, mutation and sexual reproduction as sources of variation, then describe natural selection with numbers. In high school they name the factors behind evolution and explain adaptation. The order follows the core idea codes LS3.A, LS3.B, LS4.B and LS4.C that NGSS gives each expectation.
threads.teachingPrompt: At which grade does the path first need the idea that some individuals leave more offspring than others? Does 3-LS4-2 already carry it?
gaps: None of the grade K-5 expectations in this space uses the word evolution or natural selection.
The idea that populations change over generations is first stated in middle school (MS-LS4-6).

stations.note: Grade 1: young plants and animals are like their parents but differ
Grade 3: traits are inherited and vary within a group
Grade 3: variation can help survival, finding mates and reproducing
Grade 3: some organisms survive a habitat better than others
Middle school: sexual reproduction produces genetic variation
Middle school: genetic variation raises some individuals' survival chances
Middle school: natural selection with mathematical models
High school: sources of inheritable variation
High school: advantageous heritable traits become more common
High school: four factors behind evolution
High school: natural selection leads to adaptation

threads.title: Fossils, relatedness and deep time from grade 3 to grade 12
threads.connectingIdea: How do students come to see the fossil record and body similarities as evidence that living things share ancestors?
threads.narrative: In grade 3 fossils tell students about organisms and places of long ago. In middle school students place events on the geologic time scale, read patterns of change in the fossil record and compare bodies and embryos across species to infer relationships. In high school they pull the lines of evidence together, weigh how environmental change can lead to new species and extinctions, and look at how Earth's systems and life changed together. The order follows the core idea codes LS4.A, LS4.C and ESS1.C that NGSS gives each expectation.
threads.teachingPrompt: Which expectation first lets students say that two species share an ancestor? Is the step from fossils to relatedness made explicit anywhere before middle school?
gaps: No expectation in this space asks students to read or build a family tree of species.
Deep time appears only as the geologic time scale in MS-ESS1-4.

Middle school: the geologic time scale and rock layers
Middle school: the fossil record shows change of life forms
Middle school: embryo similarities show relationships
Middle school: anatomy shows evolutionary relationships
High school: multiple lines of evidence for common ancestry and evolution
High school: environmental change, new species and extinction
High school: Earth's systems and life coevolve
